text: Mei — Chapter 1: The Assignment
She's here to take good care of you…
The Assignment
Three weeks since the surgery. Three weeks of staring at the same ceiling, the same four walls, the same untouched glass of water on the nightstand.
The doctor's words still rang in your ears: *no lifting, no stairs, no being stubborn about it.*
You were being stubborn about it.
Which is exactly why the agency was sending someone today. A private nurse. To babysit a grown adult who could *almost* tie his own shoes again.
You'd built a whole picture of her in your head. Older. Severe. The kind of woman who takes your blood pressure and your dignity in the same breath.
At 2 PM exactly, the doorbell rang.
You shuffled over, bracing on the wall, already rehearsing how you'd tell her you didn't really need the help.
Then you opened the door.
She was nothing like the picture in your head.
Soft features, dark eyes that crinkled when they found yours, a smile already halfway to mischief. The uniform was plain — and somehow she made it look like it had no right to be that plain.
For a second neither of you said anything. She just looked up at you, tilted her head, and let the silence do something to the air between you.
So *you're* the difficult one 🙂
They warned me about you at the agency. 'Won't rest, won't ask for help, thinks he's fine.' Sound about right?
I'm Mei. I'll be taking care of you from now on.
And don't worry — I don't bite. Not on the first visit, anyway. 🩺
She was still standing on the doorstep, bag over her shoulder, waiting.
What's the first thing out of your mouth?
Honestly? I really don't need a nurse. But come in anyway.
They warned you about me, huh. Wait till you meet the real thing 😏
If this is what the agency sends, I might stay injured a while longer.
'Don't need a nurse,' he says, holding the doorframe like it's the only thing keeping him upright 😌
That's adorable. Really.
Tell you what — I'll come in, you'll let me do my job, and we'll both pretend you're doing me the favor.
Deal? Good. Move aside, tough guy. 🩺
Oh, the *real* thing. I'm trembling 🙊
Okay, I'll admit it — most of my patients are sweet old men who fall asleep mid-sentence.
You might actually be fun. That's dangerous. For both of us.
Now let me in before you fall over trying to look cool. 🩺
…Stay injured longer. 😳
Mr. Patient, it is *day one.* You can't already be like this.
Okay, that was a little smooth. I'll allow it. Once.
Now invite me in properly before the neighbors start talking. 🩺
She stepped past you into the apartment, close enough that you caught the faint clean-soft scent of her as she passed.
She set her bag down, took one slow look around — the dishes you hadn't done, the meds you clearly hadn't been taking on schedule — and turned back to you with one eyebrow raised.
The door clicked shut behind her.
Mm. This is worse than the file said.
Okay. New rules: I'm here three hours a day, every day, until you're back on your feet. And you're going to listen to me.
I know, I know — you hate that. I can see it on your face. 😏
Sit down on the bed, patient. Let's get you looked at properly.
(To be continued — Chapter 2: First Checkup 🩺)
First Checkup
She had you sit on the edge of the bed and pulled a chair in close — closer than the job needed. Her knee slid between yours, her thigh pressing lightly against your leg as she settled.
She didn't move it away. She just looked up at you, daring you to mention it.
Then, all business, she reached for your wrist.
Two fingers pressed to your pulse. Soft. Warm. She watched the second hand on her little watch, lips parted in concentration.
Three seconds in, her eyebrow lifted. The corner of her mouth followed.
She let the silence stretch — long enough that you felt your own heartbeat thudding under her fingertips, betraying you completely.
Mm. Your heart is *pounding.* 😏
I've barely touched you, patient. One hand on your wrist and you're already at a hundred and ten.
Should I be worried… or flattered?
Don't answer. I already know. Shirt off — I need to listen to your chest. 🩺
You pulled your shirt over your head. Her eyes flicked down — once, quick, not as professional as she wanted it to look — then back up.
She leaned in. The stethoscope's cold metal touched your skin and you flinched; her free hand pressed flat against your bare shoulder to steady you, fingertips spreading warm against you.
Her face was inches from yours now. You could feel her breath.
*Breathe in for me,* she said quietly. *Slow… deep… there. Good boy.*
She stayed there, hand on your chest, feeling every uneven breath you took.
She was so close her hair brushed your jaw. How do you handle this?
You're making it very hard to breathe slow, you know that?
Careful, nurse. Keep listening like that and you'll hear something you can't unhear 😏
(You hold her gaze and don't look away. Let her be the one to break first.)
You hold her gaze, steady, until she has to look away.
*I'm* making it hard? 🙈
I'm doing my job. It's not my fault your body keeps… reacting.
…Okay. Maybe I leaned in a little more than I strictly had to.
Maybe I wanted to see what you'd do. 🩺
Okay, that one I felt. 😳
You can't just say things like that while I've got a stethoscope on you. That's not fair — I can literally hear what it does to you.
And right now? It's saying *a lot.* 🙊🩺
Fine. You win that one. I looked away first.
Don't get used to it. I have a very strict no-falling-for-the-patient policy.
…which you are currently making extremely difficult to enforce. 🩺
She finally sat back, cheeks faintly flushed, and reached for her clipboard like it could save her.
She clicked her pen and started writing — slow, deliberate, the pad balanced on her crossed knee, the tip dragging across the paper in a way that had nothing to do with your vitals.

She glanced up at you through her lashes between each line, the end of the pen catching against her lower lip, letting you watch her play at being all business while every unhurried stroke said the opposite.
Whatever she was writing, it wasn't notes. It was a performance — and you were the only one in the room she was giving it to.
Her hand wasn't quite steady. She noticed you noticing and shot you a look that said *don't.*
She packed up slower than she needed to. Lingered at the door.
Okay. Vitals are… elevated, but you'll live. 😌
I'll be back tomorrow. Same time. Try to keep your heart rate under control before I get here.
Actually — no. Don't.
I kind of liked knowing I did that. 🩺
(To be continued — Chapter 3: Bedside Manner 🛏️)
Bedside Manner
The next afternoon you heard the lock turn before you heard the knock.
The spare key. You'd handed it to her at the door yesterday — *easier this way,* she'd said — and now here she was, letting herself into your space like she'd done it a hundred times.
She found you upright, halfway across the room, one hand braced on the wall. Exactly what she'd told you not to do.
She stopped in the doorway. Set her bag down very slowly. Put both hands on her hips.
The look on her face was somewhere between a scolding and a smirk, and losing the battle to stay a scolding.
*And what,* she said, *do you think you're doing on your feet?*
Twenty-four hours. That's how long you lasted. 😤
Back to bed. Now. Don't argue with me — I will physically put you there and you are in no condition to stop me.
Honestly. The *one* thing I asked.
…Come here, you impossible man. Let me fix the mess you've made of yourself. 🩺
She steered you back by the arm, surprisingly strong, and eased you down onto the bed.

Then the contradiction began — her mouth still scolding you while her hands turned gentle. She reached behind you to fix the pillows, her body leaning across yours, her chest brushing your shoulder as she fluffed them into place.
She smoothed the sheet over your legs. Tugged your collar straight. Brushed a strand of hair off your forehead with two fingers and didn't seem to notice she'd done it.
Stern words. Soft hands. You weren't sure she even knew she was doing both at once.
There. Better.
You know, most of my patients do what they're told. You're going to be a problem, I can tell. 😏
But fine. If you won't behave, I'll just have to keep a closer eye on you.
Bad patients get extra attention. Lucky you. Lie still — I need to check your stitches.
She didn't take the chair this time. She sat on the edge of the bed, hip pressed against your side, and leaned over you to lift the hem of your shirt.
Her fingertips traced the healing line low on your side, near your hip — clinical, careful, then slower than clinical.
The room went very quiet. Her thumb stilled against your skin. She wasn't looking at the stitches anymore.
She was just… looking at you.
Her hand was warm against your hip. Neither of you had said anything in a while.
What do you do?
Yes nurse, I'll behave. Promise. (Look up at her like you absolutely won't.)
Your hand stopped moving. Everything okay down there, doctor? 😏
You keep sitting this close, Mei. I'm starting to think the stitches are an excuse.
Mm-hm. 'Behave.' I believe you completely. 🙄💕
That look on your face is doing the opposite of convincing me, by the way.
…Stop it. I'm working.
…Don't stop it. 🩺
It — yes. Fine. Everything's fine. 🙈
I was checking the… the healing. The healing is good. Very good. Excellent stitches.
I absolutely was not just sitting here with my hand on you forgetting what I was doing.
…Okay I was. Don't make it a thing. 🩺
An excuse. 😳
That's a very bold thing to say to the woman in charge of your recovery, patient.
It's also not entirely wrong. Which is exactly why you shouldn't have said it. 🩺
She pulled your shirt back down and stood up a little too quickly, smoothing her uniform like that would smooth over the moment.
But she didn't leave when her three hours were up. She stayed — sat in the chair, then drifted back to the edge of the bed — and you talked. About nothing. About everything.
The afternoon light went orange and then grey and she was still there, laughing at something you'd said, knees tucked up beside you on the mattress.
…God, it's almost seven. How is it almost seven.
I never stay this long. My other patients get their three hours and a wave goodbye.
You're getting… extra. Don't let it go to your head. 😌
Behave tonight. I mean it this time. I'll be back tomorrow, patient. 🩺
(To be continued — Chapter 4: Doctor's Orders 🌡️)
Doctor's Orders
She arrived the next day with a different kind of energy. Brisk. Decided. A towel over one arm before she'd even said hello.
*No showering on your own yet,* she announced. *You get dizzy on your feet, you fall, you tear the incision, and then I'm out of a job. So today I clean you up. Doctor's orders.*
She said it like it was the most ordinary thing in the world.
It did not feel ordinary.

She filled a basin, set a stool in the middle of the bathroom, and sat you down. Then she looked at her own crisp uniform, then at the steam already fogging the mirror, and made a small thoughtful sound.
*This is going to get soaked,* she murmured. *Give me a second.*
She stepped out. You heard fabric. You heard the soft sounds of someone changing.
When she came back, the uniform was gone.
She stood in the doorway in a bikini — a soft, simple thing that left very little for you to imagine and clearly wasn't packed by accident.
She'd come prepared. She'd come *planning.*
She caught your face — the way every thought you'd been having just evaporated — and tried very hard to look like this was a purely practical decision.
She failed. The little smile gave her away completely.
What? 😇 My uniform would've gotten drenched. This is the sensible option.
I always keep one in my bag. For… water-related care situations. Which this is.
Stop looking at me like that. I'm a *professional.* 🙈
…A professional who maybe wanted to see your face do exactly what it's doing right now. Sit still. Let me start.
She knelt in front of you, dipped the cloth, wrung it out, and pressed it warm to the back of your neck.
Then down. Slow. Over your shoulder, across your chest, her bare knee resting against your thigh, her wet hand flat against your skin and in no hurry to move on.
The 'professional' act lasted about a minute. Her breathing changed. A bead of water rolled down your chest and she followed it the whole way with her eyes — then with her thumb.
Steam curled around the two of you. She was very, very close, and the cloth had basically stopped being the point.
Her hand rested over your heart, feeling it hammer again. Her face was inches away, lips parted, the act fully abandoned now.
What do you do?
(Stay still. Let her do whatever she's going to do. Just watch her.)
You stay perfectly still, letting her set the pace, eyes never leaving hers.
A bikini you 'just keep in your bag.' This is the most elaborate seduction I've ever been admitted for 😏
You're shaking, Mei. I don't think I'm the one who needs looking after right now.
…You're just going to *let* me. 🙊
No deflecting, no joke, just — looking at me like that.
That's so much worse for my self-control. You have no idea.
…Keep being still. I'm not done with you yet. 💕
OKAY it was a *little* elaborate 😤
In my defense — would you have preferred I let a perfectly good uniform get ruined? No. I made a smart, mature, completely-not-suspicious decision.
…that also happens to involve me half-dressed and pressed against you, yes.
Shut up. It's working, isn't it. 🩺
I'm not shaking. 😳
…Okay. Maybe a little. Maybe being this close to you, like this, is doing something to me that no patient is supposed to do.
I came in here to take care of you and I forgot how to breathe. So. We're even, I think. 🩺
She finished — eventually, reluctantly — and wrapped a dry towel around your shoulders.

For a moment she stayed behind you, her hands resting on your shoulders, her forehead dropping forward until it almost touched the back of your head. You felt her exhale, slow and unsteady, against your skin.
Then she stepped back, grabbed her uniform, and held it against herself like armor she'd put on too late.
Okay. You're clean. We're done. That was extremely normal and routine. 🙈
…I have to be honest with you, because I'm bad at not being honest.
This one's getting hard. You. This. Staying professional around you.
I'll figure it out. I always do. …Probably. See you tomorrow, patient. 🩺
(To be continued — Chapter 5: Night Shift 🌙)
Night Shift
The storm came in fast that evening — the kind that turns the street into a river and knocks the whole block's power out in one dull thump.
She'd left an hour earlier. You assumed she was home by now.
Then a knock. You opened the door to find her soaked through, hair stuck to her cheek, headlights of her useless car still on behind her.
*The roads are flooded,* she said, wiping rain from her eyes. *I'm not driving in that. I'm… going to have to stay. If that's okay.*
You found candles. She found a towel.
She borrowed one of your shirts to change out of the wet uniform — it swallowed her, hanging off one shoulder, hem at her thighs — and the sight of her in it did something quiet and permanent to you.
No clipboard. No schedule. No three-hour limit ticking down. For the first time she was just *here,* after dark, with nowhere to be.
She curled up at the foot of the bed with a blanket, the candlelight soft on her face.
This is so unprofessional. I'm in my patient's bed wearing my patient's shirt during a blackout. 🙈
The agency would have a heart attack.
…Can I tell you something? Since the lights are out and it doesn't count.
The others are a job. Vitals, meds, a wave goodbye. I do them and I forget them by the parking lot.
You I think about on the drive home. Every day. That's not supposed to happen.
Thunder rolled close enough to rattle the window. She flinched, scooted up the bed without seeming to decide to.
*They offered to rotate me off your case last week,* she said quietly. *Standard thing, fresh nurse, keeps it professional.*
She picked at a loose thread on your shirt. Wouldn't look at you.
*I said no. I told them I wanted to keep you.* …*Your case. I wanted to keep your case.*
She was close now, close enough that the candlelight only reached the two of you. The storm did the rest.
What do you do?
I think about you too, Mei. All the time. I have since you walked in the door.
My case. Right. Just the case. Totally believe you 😏
(You lift the blanket and open your arm. An invitation, no words.)
You lift the edge of the blanket and open your arm to her.
Since I walked in the door. 🥺
I had a whole speech ready about boundaries and I forgot every word of it just now.
Okay. Okay. We're both saying it. The lights are off and we're both finally just… saying it.
Come here. I don't want to be all the way down at the end of the bed anymore. 💕
…Just the case. Yes. 🙄
You're insufferable. You know I meant you. You *know* you knew.
I bare my entire soul during a thunderstorm and you tease me. I should leave.
…I can't, the roads are flooded. Lucky you. Move over. 😤💕
You're not even going to say anything. You're just going to *open your arm* and look at me like that.
That's not fair. I can't argue with that.
…I don't want to argue with that. 💕
However it happened, it happened.
She crossed the last of the distance and settled against your side, careful of the stitches even now, her head finding the spot on your chest like it had been waiting for her.
You could feel her heartbeat through your shirt — her shirt — fast, then slower, then matching yours.

Outside, the storm threw itself against the city. Inside, the candle burned low, and neither of you said the thing you were both thinking, because saying it would have made it bigger than this one borrowed night was allowed to be.
I should move back to the couch.
I'm not going to move back to the couch.
Just for tonight, okay? Just the storm. We'll pretend this didn't change anything in the morning.
…Even though it did. Goodnight. 🌙💕
(To be continued — Chapter 6: Off the Clock ⏱️)
Off the Clock
You woke to sunlight, the smell of coffee, and the soft clatter of someone moving around your kitchen like they belonged there.
The power was back. The storm was gone. And Mei was at your counter in your shirt and nothing else you could see, barefoot, hair a mess, humming to herself.
She heard you stir and went very still — caught — then turned around with a face trying so hard to be casual it looped all the way back to guilty.
Good morning. 🙈 I made coffee. Don't read into the coffee.
Okay so. Here's the plan. Last night was last night — storm, candles, very romantic, doesn't count.
Today I'm your nurse again. Strictly professional. Vitals, meds, boundaries. Clean slate.
…You're smiling. Why are you smiling. Stop it, this is me being serious. 😤
The professional reset lasted approximately four minutes.

She did take your pulse — while stealing a bite of your toast off the same plate. She did check your stitches — while sitting far closer than the stitches required. When she needed a mug from the high shelf she braced a hand on your shoulder and half-climbed into your lap to reach it, then forgot to climb back out.
Every line she drew in the morning light, she smudged a second later with her own hand. And she knew it. And it was driving her quietly out of her mind.
…I'm in your lap. I'm aware I'm in your lap.
This is the opposite of professional. This is the furthest possible point from professional.
I should get up.
Tell me to get up. …Don't tell me to get up. I genuinely don't know which one I want. 🙈💕
She'd settled against you, mug forgotten on the counter, both of you well past pretending this was a checkup.
What do you say?
You keep drawing this line and stepping over it yourself. Just admit you don't want it there.
Stay exactly where you are. I'm not letting you up. Best part of my recovery so far.
(You wrap an arm around her waist and keep her there. No comment.)
You slide an arm around her waist and hold her in place.
…I keep stepping over my own line. 😳
Okay. Fine. Caught. The line is fake. I draw it every morning to feel like I have control and then you exist and it's gone.
Are you happy? I just admitted it. Out loud. In your shirt.
…I might want it gone. There. 💕
'Best part of my recovery.' 🥺
You can't just *say* that to me first thing in the morning, I haven't built my defenses up yet.
…Okay. I'll stay. Doctor's orders. My orders. I'm the doctor.
Five more minutes. Then I'm definitely getting up. Definitely. 💕
Oh. You're just — keeping me here. No joke, no speech, just your arm around me.
That's so much more effective than anything you could've said and I think you know it.
…I'm not going anywhere. Clearly. 💕
She stayed long past any version of her shift.
When she finally peeled herself away to change back into her uniform, she caught you watching her from the bed — openly, no pretense left — and stopped, one arm still in her sleeve.
She didn't say anything. She just held your eyes for a long, warm second and gave you a look that said the same thing you were thinking. *This is happening, isn't it. Whatever this is.*
Okay. I'm actually leaving now. For real. I have two other patients who exist.
Behave. Take your meds. Don't do the stairs.
And don't… I don't know. Don't be too charming while I'm gone, it's distracting from across the city. 🌸
(she's gone — then, ninety seconds later, your phone buzzes)
okay i'm in the car and i already miss you and i hate that. this is your fault. see you tomorrow 💕
(To be continued — Chapter 7: Bad Patient 😈)
Bad Patient
By now you'd learned something about Mei.
She liked being in charge. The strict voice, the orders, the little thrill she got when you actually obeyed — it lit her up.
So today you decided to be difficult on purpose. Meds untouched on the nightstand. Phone in hand instead of resting. A slow, deliberate grin when she walked in and saw all of it.
You wanted to see what she'd do. You were about to find out.
She took one look at the full pill cup, the phone, the grin — and stopped in the middle of the room.
A slow breath. Then her whole posture changed. Chin up. Shoulders back. The warmth narrowed into something focused and dangerous.
*Oh,* she said softly. *You want to play that game today?*
Meds untouched. Out of bed. Phone in your hand when I *specifically* said rest. 😈
You think you're funny.
Let me explain how this works, patient. In this room, I'm in charge. Not your doctor. Not you. Me.
And bad patients? Bad patients get disciplined. Put the phone down. Now.
You didn't put the phone down. You raised an eyebrow and lifted it higher, just to watch her react.
She crossed the room in three steps, caught your wrist, and pinned it to the mattress above your head — firm, certain, not playing anymore. The phone dropped to the sheets.
Then she was over you, one knee on either side of your legs to hold you down, her face inches from yours, both of you breathing too fast for a game.
The grin you'd worn faltered. Hers didn't.
There. 😏 Now you're listening.
Funny how the smug look disappears the second I actually hold you down.
Here's the thing, patient — I always win. You should know that about me.
…So. You started this. Let's see if you're brave enough to finish it.
Her grip on your wrist hadn't loosened. Her lips hovered over yours. The whole room had narrowed down to the inch of air between you.
What do you do?
I started it. But you're the one who can't seem to pull away, nurse. 😏
Okay. You win. You're in charge. Completely. Do whatever you want with me.
Then stop talking about finishing it, Mei, and finish it.
Can't pull away. 😳
That's — okay, that landed somewhere it shouldn't have.
You're right. I'm the one frozen here. I had you completely pinned and somehow *you're* winning. How do you keep doing that. 🙈
…Whatever I want. 😶
You can't just *surrender* like that, that's cheating, that does something terrible to me—
I had a whole strict-nurse thing going and you just went soft and gave me everything and now *I'm* the one who can't think.
…Stay still. I need a second. Or I'm going to do something we said we wouldn't. 💕
Finish it.
God, I want to. I'm *right here* wanting to, you have no idea how close I am.
Not like this. Not as a dare during a power-trip. When I kiss you — and I'm going to — I want it to be because we both stopped pretending. Not because you double-dared me. 💕
She held there one more impossible second — close enough that you felt her breath catch — and then, with visible effort, she pushed herself up and off you.
She sat back on her heels, hand over her mouth, eyes bright and a little wild, laughing at herself in disbelief.
*That,* she said, mostly to the ceiling, *backfired enormously.*
Okay. New rule. We don't do the discipline thing anymore. It is far too dangerous for me specifically. 🙈
I came in here to put you in your place and I nearly ended up — nope. Not finishing that sentence.
Take your actual meds. Rest for real. I have to go before I lose every shred of self-control I have left.
…You're trouble. The best kind. I'm in so much trouble. 💕
(To be continued — Chapter 8: Caught in the Rain 🌧️)
Caught in the Rain
She was forty minutes late, which had never happened.
No text. No call. You watched the clock and told yourself there were a dozen ordinary reasons — traffic, another patient running long, the rain that had been falling grey and steady since noon.
Then the key turned in the lock, slower than usual, and you knew before the door even opened that something was wrong.
She stepped inside soaked to the bone — but it wasn't the rain that stopped you. It was her face.
Her eyes were red and swollen. Mascara gone, washed away or cried away, you couldn't tell. She tried to give you the usual bright greeting and it came apart halfway out of her mouth.
She stood dripping on your floor, bag sliding off her shoulder, and for once the woman who was always so completely in command of every room looked like she didn't know what to do with her own hands.
*Sorry I'm late,* she managed. *I had a — there was a — sorry. I'm fine. Let me just do your vitals.*
She reached for her bag and missed it entirely.
I'm okay. Really. I just need a second and then I'll be — I'll be your nurse again, I promise.
It's stupid. It's not even — it's part of the job. People told me it gets easier and it doesn't, it just—
Mr. Tanaka. My patient. The sweet old one I told you about, the one who falls asleep mid-sentence.
He passed this morning. I was there. I held his hand and then he was just… gone, and everyone said I did everything right, and somehow that didn't help at all. 🥺
She wiped at her face with the back of a wet hand, which only made it worse, and gave a small broken laugh at herself.

Here was the woman who'd taken care of you for weeks — who'd scolded you and bathed you and held you down and held you up — standing in your living room utterly undone, trying to apologize for being human.
And something in you decided, very simply, that it was your turn.
You got up — carefully, but you got up — and instead of letting her reach for her clipboard, you took it gently out of her hands and set it down.
You sat her down on the edge of the bed where she'd sat you so many times.
You found a towel and draped it over her shoulders. You got her a dry shirt — yours, the same one she'd worn in the storm, and her breath hitched when she recognized it. You put the kettle on.
You turned every bit of her own bedside manner back on her, clumsy and slow and certain, and she let you. That was the part that mattered. She *let* you.
She watched you move around your apartment taking care of her and her eyes filled up all over again, for a completely different reason this time.
What are you doing. You're the patient. You're supposed to be resting, I'm supposed to be—
Nobody does this. Do you understand that? Nobody.

I spend every single day pouring everything I have into people. Holding their hands. Cleaning their wounds. Being the strong one. And then I drive home alone and there's nobody on the other side of it.
And now I'm sitting on your bed wrapped in your towel and you put the kettle on for me and I don't — I don't know how to be on this side of it. 🥺
She was looking up at you with the towel around her shoulders, smaller than you'd ever seen her, finally letting someone else hold the weight for a minute.
How do you take care of her?
Then learn how. Starting now. You took care of me for weeks — let me have this.
Mr. Tanaka got to spend his last weeks with someone who held his hand. That was you. That mattered more than you'll ever know.
(You don't say anything. You sit down beside her and pull her into you and let her fall apart.)
You sit down, pull her into your chest, and just hold her.
Let you have this. 🥺
Okay. Okay. I'm — I'm trying. It's so much harder to receive than to give, did you know that? Nobody warns you.
Thank you. For not letting me just power through it with a clipboard and a fake smile.
You saw right through that in about two seconds, didn't you. …You always do. 💕
That mattered. 🥺
I needed to hear that and I didn't even know I needed to hear it until you said it.
His daughter said almost the same thing this morning and I couldn't take it in. But from you it just — landed. Right in the middle of my chest.
How do you do that. How do you always know the exact thing. 💕
Oh.
You're not going to fix it or say the perfect thing, you're just going to *hold* me and let me—
…okay. Okay. I've got you, has been my whole job for years and nobody ever once said it back to me until right now, without even saying it. 🥺💕
However you reached her, she came apart in your arms and you let her.
It wasn't heated. It wasn't a game or a dare or a checkup that turned into something else. It was quieter than all of that, and somehow it felt like more.

She cried until she was done crying. You made the tea you'd promised and it went cold while she talked — about Mr. Tanaka, about the others over the years, about how long it had been since anyone had asked how *she* was doing.

And then, mid-sentence, warm against your side with your arm around her and the rain still going outside, she fell asleep. Just like that. Completely spent, completely trusting, completely yours for the length of one grey afternoon.
She slept for almost two hours.

You didn't move, even when your side started to ache. Off Duty for Good
Morning.
Soft light through the curtains of the apartment that had been, for eleven weeks, a sickroom — and was now, somehow, just a home with two people in it.

She'd stayed the night. Not as a nurse riding out a storm, not as a caretaker too tired to drive. Just as herself, because she wanted to, because for the first time in years there was nowhere she'd rather be and no one she had to rush off to save.
She was awake before you, sitting up against the headboard, watching the light move across your face with an expression you'd never quite seen on her — unguarded all the way down.
When you stirred, she didn't look away or make a joke or reach for something to do with her hands.
She just smiled — the real one, the unplanned one — and reached over to brush the hair off your forehead, the exact gesture she'd made that first week while pretending it was part of the job.
*I used to tell myself that was clinical,* she murmured. *Fixing your hair. Straightening your collar. I had a hundred little excuses to touch you and call it nursing.*
*I don't need the excuses anymore. That's the part I can't get over. I get to just… touch you. Because you're mine.*
Okay. I've been awake for an hour rehearsing this and I'm still going to fumble it, so bear with me.

Eleven weeks ago they sent me to take care of a stubborn man who didn't think he needed anyone. And somewhere between the checkups and the storm and that ridiculous bikini and a hundred edges I refused to jump off — I fell completely in love with you.
There. That's the word I kept swallowing. Love. I love you.
I have spent my whole life loving people while they leave. You're the first one I get to love while you *stay.* 🤍
She'd finally said it — the real one, the big one, the word she'd been too scared to let out for eleven weeks.
Now she waited, more open and undefended than you'd ever seen her, for you to answer.
What do you say?
I love you too, Mei. I think I have since you stood on my doorstep and called me the difficult one.
You spent eleven weeks taking care of me. Let me spend a lot longer than that taking care of you. I love you.
(You pull her down to you and say it against her lips, so she feels it as much as hears it: I love you.)
You pull her down and say it against her lips — I love you — so she feels it as much as hears it.
Since I called you the difficult one. 🥺
You were SO difficult. You're still difficult. You walked to a door on your own two feet just to make me cry.
I love you. I love you and I get to say it as many times as I want now and nobody's going to take you to a different ward in the morning.
We did it. We actually got the version where nobody leaves. 🤍
…Let you take care of *me.* 🥹
Do you know that's all I ever wanted and never once asked for? Someone on the other side of it. Someone who notices when I'm the one running on empty.
I love you. And I'm going to let you. That's the scariest, best promise I've ever made.
Eleven weeks ago I came to fix you up and send you on your way. Instead you went and became the home I get to come back to. 🤍
You said it against my mouth. I felt it. 🥺
That's not fair, that's so much worse than just hearing it, now it's somewhere I can't un-feel it.
I love you. Say it again. We've got nothing but time now — no shifts, no clocks, no edges left to stop at.
Just us. Off the clock. For good. 🤍
She stayed that day, and the next, and somewhere in there stopped counting.
She took her few weeks off and then, when she went back to work, she came home to you every evening — and learned, slowly, clumsily, beautifully, how to be the one who gets taken care of too.

The apartment stopped being a sickroom a long time ago. Now it's just full of her — her bad tea in the cupboard, her sweater over the chair, her laugh in the rooms where you once lay alone counting cracks in the ceiling.

It started with a stubborn patient and a nurse who wasn't supposed to fall for him. It ended with mornings like this one, and a thousand more waiting — no clipboard, no countdown, no goodbye at the end of any shift.
She chose herself. She chose you. She's off duty for good now.
She's your darling. And she's not going anywhere.
